fields.h1: Build a Meeting Request Form That Moves Requests to a Decision
fields.hero_description: Build a meeting request form that routes each request to the right approver and keeps every answer in a database you own.
fields.features_heading: What Happens After Someone Asks for Time
fields.features_subheading: A meeting request form earns its place when the person asking hears back. Emergent builds these six parts around that answer.
fields.feature_1:
A purpose question that names the decision

The form asks what the meeting needs to decide, how long it should run, and who has to attend. A request that only says "catch up" is easy to spot and easy to redirect.
fields.feature_2:
Approvers picked by amount or by person

You describe the rule in plain English, such as a budget threshold or a named executive, and Emergent builds the approval step around it. Change the threshold later by asking.
fields.feature_3:
Sections that appear only when they apply

An in-person meeting needs a room, food, and parking. A video call needs none of that, so the form shows those sections only to the in-person requests and skips them for calls.
fields.feature_4:
Approved meetings on the shared calendar

The app connects to the calendar tool already in use through its API. An approved request becomes a calendar entry with its time and attendees, and nobody types it in twice.
fields.feature_5:
Slack and email updates for both sides

Approvers get a Slack or email alert when a request is waiting on them. The requester gets an email each time the status changes, with the reason written out when it is a no.
fields.feature_6:
Every request in a database you own

Responses are stored in a database you own, with no cap on how many meeting requests the form accepts. On paid plans, the full code also exports to your GitHub repository.

fields.usecase_heading: Where Four Meeting Requests Went Next
fields.tab_content_1:
Above $10,000, it waits for finance

Dervla Haukeland, a sales director at Stellwick Coatings, asks for a 2-day offsite for 24 people with an $18,000 budget. Any request over $10,000 goes to finance first, and this one lands with Feodor Zuberi. He approves it on Tuesday, and only then does it reach the meetings team.
fields.tab_content_2:
CEO requests that name no decision go to a delegate

In May, Lochmere Freight's chief of staff, Gwilym Pomeroy, got 26 requests to meet the CEO. The form asks which decision the CEO has to make. The 9 requests that named none were offered a meeting with a delegate. The other 17 went on the CEO's list, Bryn Merriwell's Q3 carrier contract among them.
fields.tab_content_3:
Virtual reviews never see a room or catering question

Mateus Vasquez-Lund runs design reviews at Inkpen & Rowe Architects. He requests a 45-minute review for 6 attendees and picks Virtual on the first screen. The form drops the room and catering questions and moves straight to the agenda and the pre-read upload. His request goes in with the review deck attached.
fields.tab_content_4:
Every pending request in one Monday message

Lunmark Instruments plans customer visits and team offsites through one meetings desk. Every Monday at 9:00 am, the app posts a Slack message to #meetings-desk listing the 6 requests still pending. The 2 that start within 14 days sit at the top of the list, and Cosima Rendell's customer visit, 5 days out, is first.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Meeting Request Form
fields.howto_description: Follow 7 steps to build a meeting request form that sends each request to its approver and onto the calendar.
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Describe the form in a prompt
fields.howto_step_1_des: List every person who approves meetings and the rule that sends a request to them, such as a budget line or a named executive. Settle those rules on paper before you open the builder.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Make the first required question ask what the meeting has to decide. Requesters who cannot answer it in a sentence are the ones a shorter call or a delegate can help.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Tell Emergent who fills the form in, what each answer is for, and where approved requests go. Emergent builds the form, the database behind it, and a dashboard of requests.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Ask for each rule in plain words, with its exact threshold. Name the approver, the backup when that person is away, and what the requester sees while the request waits.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Put the format question near the top. Ask Emergent to show the room and catering questions only for in-person meetings, and the agenda upload for every format.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Connect the calendar tool so approved meetings land there with their attendees. Then ask for the Slack alerts approvers need and the Monday digest of pending requests.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Send one request under your budget threshold, one over it, and one with no decision named. Check that each lands with the right person before you share the link.

faq_plan.q: What is a meeting request form?
faq_plan.ref: What is a meeting request form?

prov.original: What is a meeting request form?

faq_plan.a: A meeting request form is the form someone fills in to ask for time with a person, a team, or a group that plans meetings. It records who is asking, what the meeting is for, how long it should take, and who should attend. A good one ends with an answer: approved, declined, or redirected to someone better placed.

faq_plan.q: How do I create a meeting request form?
faq_plan.a: Decide who approves which requests, then describe the form, the approval rules, and the alerts in one prompt to Emergent's AI form builder. Emergent turns that prompt into the form, its database, the routing logic, and a dashboard of requests. Change any part later by asking for it in plain English.

faq_plan.q: When is a meeting request form template not enough?
faq_plan.a: It stops being enough once a request has to reach an approver or land on a calendar. Use a meeting request form template when all you need is a record of who asked and when. Once routing matters, build the form with the approval rules behind its fields, and keep the template's questions as your starting list.

faq_plan.q: What fields should a meeting request form ask for?
faq_plan.a: Ask for the purpose, the decision needed, the length, the attendees, the format, and two or three preferred dates. Add budget and headcount only for events that cost money. That is more than a sign up form asks. Make only the purpose and the dates required, and leave the rest optional.

faq_plan.q: How can a meeting request form send requests to different approvers?
faq_plan.a: Write each routing rule as a plain condition, such as a budget over a set amount or a request addressed to a named executive, and name the approver for it. Give every rule a backup approver for weeks when that person is away. Emergent builds those rules into the form, and you change one by asking.

faq_plan.q: How much notice should a meeting request form ask for?
faq_plan.a: Set the notice period by meeting type and show it on the form, for example 2 business days for a 30-minute call and 6 weeks for an offsite. Then have the date picker hide dates inside that window. Requesters see the rule before they pick a date, and nobody gets a no for a reason they never saw.

faq_plan.q: How is a meeting request form different from a form that books client sessions?
faq_plan.a: It asks for time instead of booking it. A consultation form books a client into a session with a provider, and the provider has already agreed to offer that time. A meeting request asks for time that someone still has to approve. Its answers go to an approver first and a calendar second.

faq_plan.q: Can a meeting request form show requesters where their request stands?
faq_plan.a: Yes, if you ask for a status page or status emails when you build the form. The app can email the requester each time the status changes, from received to approved or declined. Put the reason in the decline email. The requester then knows whether to try a delegate or a later date.

faq_plan.q: How should a meeting request form store its responses?
faq_plan.a: Keep each request as one record that carries its status and its approver, in a database you own instead of a shared spreadsheet. Forms built with Emergent have no response caps. Record the date each request was approved as well, and you can report how long requests waited.

faq_plan.q: Should employees and outside visitors use the same meeting request form?
faq_plan.a: Use two forms when the two groups need different routing. Employees asking for budget or an executive's time need approval steps; outside visitors need a quick reply. A visitor who only wants information belongs on a lead capture form, which keeps the meeting queue for real meeting requests.

plan.angle: The live top 10 splits two ways: event-management pages on forms that collect meeting details for a meetings team (three of the ten results come from one event platform), and static PDFs or form templates for asking an office or a board for time. None of them shows what happens to a request after submit. This page wins by building a meeting request form that carries each request to a decision: budgets over a set amount wait for a finance approver, requests to meet an executive that name no decision go to a delegate, virtual requests skip the room questions, and a Monday digest shows the meetings team what is still pending, with every request in a database the team owns.
